slides.page_title: Auth Basics: Steps, Carriers & Bearer Tokens

items: Every request stands alone, no memory of the last
So a credential must ride on each one
Conflating the three steps is where auth bugs start
Know: password, PIN
Have: TOTP app, security key
Are: fingerprint, face
MFA = two categories, not two passwords
Whoever holds the token IS the user
No proof of possession is ever demanded
Theft = full takeover until exp or revocation

blocks.title: The Two Threats This Book Fights
items: Token theft: XSS, log leaks, sniffing
Token misuse by a third-party site: CSRF
Every flag ahead maps to one of these

blocks.title: Ground Rules
items: TLS is a prerequisite, not a feature
No HTTPS = every scheme here falls to a sniffer
Never trust what the client can edit
No userId in hidden fields, no isAdmin in localStorage

blocks.title: Auth != Session Management
blocks.text: Checking a password once is easy. Keeping someone safely logged in for 30 days is the actual hard problem.

items: sid = >=128 bits from a CSPRNG, opaque
Never a sequential integer or hash(userId)
Session data never leaves the server
Cookie is a pointer, so payload size is free
Absolute lifetime: hard cap, e.g. 30 days
Idle timeout: sliding, e.g. 2 h of silence
Implement both, not one
Redis TTL gives you the idle clock for free
Deletion is instant, everywhere, one command
That is the big advantage over stateless tokens
Fixation: attacker plants a known sid pre-login
Fix: regenerate sid on login, logout, role change

blocks.note: planted pre-login sid is now dead

blocks.title: Log Out All Other Devices
blocks.text: SMEMBERS the user's session set, DEL every sid except the current one, then prune the set. Run it on every password change too.

blocks.title: Cost & Hybrids
items: Every request hits the store (~0.2 ms Redis GET)
Cheap, but a hard dependency and a SPOF
Signed cookie stores (Rails, Flask) keep state client-side
Same revocation problem: treat them as tokens

slides.page_title: JWT Header: kid, Encoding & What Stays Out

items: Header carries alg and optionally kid
kid names the signing key: that is what enables rotation
base64url is encoding, not encryption
Never put secrets, PII or password hashes inside

rows: one service, you own all of it

blocks.title: Verify In This Order
blocks.text: Check alg against an allowlist, then the signature, then exp/nbf/iss/aud. Reading claims before verifying is exactly how bugs get in.

items: alg: none, attacker strips the signature entirely
Vulnerable libraries happily accept it
HS/RS confusion: re-sign with the public key as HMAC secret
A library that infers alg from the header verifies it

lines: // pinned: header alg is never trusted

items: JWS: signed, readable, what 'JWT' means in practice
JWE: encrypted, opaque, only when the client must not read it

lines: # verifiers fetch + cache: OIDC rotates live
// edit sub, and you trust it

items: HS256 secret: ==≥256 bits== of real randomness
Never reuse it as any other app secret
Every HS256 verifier can also **mint** tokens

blocks.title: Pin, Then Trust
blocks.text: The token never chooses its own algorithm. Your verifier config does.

blocks.title: Clock Skew
items: Allow ~30-60 s leeway on exp and nbf
nbf = not before, iat = issued at
No leeway: drift causes intermittent 401s
Hard to reproduce, easy to prevent

slides.page_title: Sessions vs JWT: The Real Trade-off

blocks.text: 3. Sessions vs JWT, Row By Row

items: Session data is read fresh: permission changes bite instantly
JWT claims are a snapshot, stale until expiry
JWT 'logout' only deletes the client copy
A stolen token still works, so short exp is the only fix

blocks.title: The Complexity Bill
items: Sessions: one library, one Redis
JWT: alg pinning, key rotation, clock skew
Plus refresh flows and a revocation story
Big JWTs can also blow past proxy header limits
First-party web app, one backend, use sessions
Mobile or third-party API clients, use JWT
Many services verifying without a shared DB, use JWT
Keep the access token short-lived either way

blocks.title: Why The Hybrid Wins
blocks.text: Revocation of sessions plus statelessness of JWT: the refresh token is server-stored and killable, the access token needs no I/O to verify.

items: Long-lived JWT, 7-30 days, parked in localStorage
Unrevocable and XSS-readable at the same time
Worst half of both models, sold as 'stateless auth'
Lax still sends on top-level GET navigations
Strict means an email link lands the user logged out
None without Secure is rejected by browsers
Omit Domain: host-only cookie, the safe default
Domain=example.com shares it with blog.example.com
Path=/ is not a security boundary, the DOM reads across paths
Omit Max-Age and Expires: dies with the browser process
Chrome session-restore can keep it alive anyway
__Host- forces Secure + Path=/ + no Domain
So it is host-locked, immune to subdomain injection
__Secure- only forces Secure
Browsers reject non-conforming sets: a free integrity check

blocks.title: Cookies Ignore Ports
items: localhost:3000 and :4000 share one jar
Scheme barely separates them either
Cookie isolation is weaker than same-origin policy in JS
Partitioned gives a separate jar per top-level site
The replacement path as third-party cookies are phased out
CSRF is a write attack, not a read attack
The same-origin policy blocks reading the response
Triggering the side effect is enough: transfers, password and email changes
The browser attaches your cookies to requests started by any site
evil.com submits a form to bank.com/transfer
It arrives fully authenticated, because ambient credentials
Only cookie-based, ambient auth
Authorization: Bearer is never attached automatically
So header-token APIs are structurally CSRF-immune

rows: random token bound to session, in the form
same value as cookie and field, compared

items: Reject state-changing requests whose Origin is not allowlisted
Handle a missing Origin explicitly, never allow by default
For JSON APIs require a custom header like X-Requested-With
Simple cross-site requests cannot set one without a preflight you refuse

blocks.title: Pick Per Stack
blocks.text: Server-rendered forms: ==synchronizer token==. JSON API: custom header plus Origin check. SameSite=Lax underneath both.

blocks.title: Not A CSRF Defense
items: CORS governs reading responses, not sending requests
A permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin makes it worse
SameSite=Lax is defense-in-depth, not a complete fix
It misses state-changing GETs and old browsers vary

slides.page_title: CSRF Hard Rules & Where To Store Tokens

items: Never make GET state-changing: a bare fires it
State-changing GETs also slip past SameSite=Lax
Protect the login form with a CSRF token too
Login CSRF logs the victim into the attacker's account, recording their activity
localStorage persists forever and is shared across all tabs
Every script reads it, including analytics and a bad npm dep
sessionStorage clears on tab close: smaller blast radius, still not safe
Access token in a JS variable or React state
Dies on refresh, invisible to document.cookie
Storage-scraping payloads find nothing
Restored by one silent refresh call on page load

blocks.title: If You Have XSS, You Already Lost
blocks.text: An attacker running script just makes authenticated requests AS the user, straight through the HttpOnly cookie. HttpOnly limits exfiltration, not abuse.

items: Which is exactly why HttpOnly still matters
Exfiltrated tokens work from the attacker's machine, forever
In-page abuse ends when the user closes the tab
That blocks injected inline script, the actual XSS payload
Your frontend supply chain is part of the auth surface
Every dependency and <script src> can read localStorage

caption.text: Most auth bugs are not exotic crypto failures, they are a missing cookie flag, an unpinned algorithm, or a token parked in localStorage for 30 days. This handbook walks the whole wire: sessions vs JWT with real numbers, every cookie attribute that matters, CSRF exploits and their actual defenses, argon2id parameters, and rotation with refresh-token reuse detection. Twelve chapters of dense notes, ending in a cheat sheet you can ship against.
